title: Write an if–then plan for your goal

body.heading: Two kinds of if–then
paragraphs: An if–then plan links a situation to an action: “If X happens, then I will Y.” For goals, two kinds earn their keep. The first is a starting plan: “If it is 7 p.m. on Tuesday, then I will open the course and do one lesson.” It gives the goal a time and place instead of a hope.

The second is a rescue plan, written for the obstacle you already know is coming: “If a meeting eats my study time, then I will do ten minutes before bed.” Obstacles stop being surprises and become scheduled events with prepared answers.

body.heading: Write them where the moment happens
paragraphs: A plan stored in a notebook you never open cannot help you at 7 p.m. Put the starting plan where the trigger lives: on the calendar, on the fridge, as the name of the alarm itself.
Keep each plan to one sentence and make the action small. “Then I will do a full workout” collapses under a tired evening; “then I will change into my kit and do five minutes” survives one.

body.heading: One goal, two plans
paragraphs: Choose your most important current goal and write exactly two sentences for it: one starting plan, one rescue plan for its most likely obstacle. That is a complete system, small enough to remember and strong enough to matter.

When a plan fires and works, notice. When it fails, edit the sentence — a different trigger, a smaller action — rather than concluding the goal is hopeless. The plan is a draft, and drafts are meant to be revised.

takeaway: Decide in advance: if this moment comes, then I will do this small thing.
